meta.regime: The regime is a triple central-bank tightening window - ECB Thursday, Fed the 16th, BoE the 17th, BoJ the 18th - running on top of a hot war in the Strait of Hormuz and a synchronised global bond selloff that is now doing its own work in FX. The important shift this morning is that being a hiking central bank no longer buys a currency anything on its own, because the market has already priced the hikes and, in the euro's case, priced the terminal too. What still pays is the RESIDUAL: where the forward path is still open (Japan, Australia), and where the bond market is repricing FISCAL risk rather than policy (the UK). That is why the whole board has compressed toward +1 and the cleanest expressions are no longer long-anything but short sterling across four legs.

dailyRead: Two things this file had wrong are corrected this morning, and both of them point at the same trade. Start with the euro, because the correction is the larger one. This file has been carrying the December ECB question as a roughly 50/50 split on a further move to 2.75%, and using that open forward path as part of the case for EUR at +2. The Reuters poll published on September 3 says otherwise and says it emphatically: all 65 economists surveyed expect a 25bp hike to a 2.50% deposit facility on Thursday September 10, but roughly 91% then expect 2.50% to be the rate at the END of this year, and 78% expect it to still be 2.50% through the middle of next year. The poll's own framing is that Thursday is the second and FINAL move in what would be the ECB's shortest hiking campaign in fifteen years, and that policymakers have little appetite to signal further tightening afterwards because long-term inflation expectations are well anchored. Under this file's own rule - an economist poll outranks a previous run's coin-flip description - that is a correction, not a nuance. EUR comes down from +2 to +1. Nothing about the euro's data has deteriorated: HICP is still 3.3%, the highest since September 2023, core 2.4%, Q2 GDP +0.4% quarterly and 1.0% annual against 0.5% previously, unemployment 6.4%, deposit facility re-verified on TE this morning at 2.25% with the main refi at 2.40% and the marginal lending rate at 2.65%. What has changed is that there is no longer a forward path left to buy. The hike is priced, the terminal is priced, and Thursday's risk is therefore asymmetric to the downside for the euro: a Lagarde press conference that confirms 2.50% as the terminal rate takes the last piece of premium out, while a hawkish surprise has to fight a 65-for-65 consensus to get paid. Own the euro against sterling and the kiwi, where the differential is structural. Stop owning it against the dollar, the Aussie and the yen, where it is now a coin flip on guidance. The second correction is a genuinely new leg and it belongs to sterling. Over the last week the gilt market led a global bond rout that has very little to do with the Bank of England's reaction function: the 10-year gilt yield climbed as much as 11 basis points to 5.25%, a post-2008 peak, and the 30-year hit 5.89%, its highest since May 1998. This is the important distinction for FX - rising yields driven by a hawkish central bank support a currency, rising yields driven by high government debt issuance and fiscal credibility questions do the opposite, and this is unambiguously the second kind. It is happening alongside, not instead of, the dovish resolution of the Bank of England trigger: the Decision Maker Panel survey cut one-year firm CPI expectations to 3.1% from 3.4% with three-year at 2.8%, and September 17 is now roughly 90% priced for no change at 3.75%, with the 6-3 July vote likely to hold or soften. UK core CPI has been flat at 2.6% for three straight months, headline is 2.9%, quarterly GDP slowed to +0.4% from +0.6%, and wage growth decelerated to 4.1% from 4.4%. So sterling now has a central bank that will not move, an inflation expectations survey that removed the hawkish case, and a bond market repricing fiscal risk into the currency. GBP goes from 0 to MINUS 1 and becomes the only negative score on this board. That is what makes today's trade list simple: GBP/JPY and GBP/AUD stay the two highest-conviction tickets at a three-notch differential, EUR/GBP is upgraded to HIGH at two notches despite the euro downgrade, GBP/USD is upgraded from MEDIUM to HIGH, and GBP/CAD and GBP/CHF both firm to MEDIUM. Four separate legs, one thesis, no dollar risk in three of them. The yen is the other side of most of those trades and it strengthened again overnight. USD/JPY is 155.865, down 0.25% on the session and 2.18% on the month, having led the majors last week. Pricing for the September 18 BoJ meeting is now roughly 80% for a hike to 1.25% on TE's own forecast, Ueda has kept the door explicitly open, and board member Takata has gone further - he says the Bank should hike NIMBLY in response to rising inflation and has suggested moves could come faster or in bigger increments than the recent semiannual pace, which is a materially more hawkish framing than a single 25bp step. The Japanese 10-year hit 3% for the first time since 1996 during the bond rout, which for Japan is a policy-normalisation signal rather than a fiscal-stress one. JPY holds +2 and stays the top of the board. The standing caveat has not improved and should not be dropped: July real household spending fell 3.6% year-on-year, the eighth consecutive decline, the trade balance is MINUS 634 billion yen and the current account swung to MINUS 92.3 billion, so the BoJ is hiking into an oil shock that strengthens its inflation argument while eroding its demand base. Average cash earnings tonight at 23:50Z, with final Q2 GDP and the current account, is the last domestic print before the meeting and the specific thing that would take JPY to +1 if it misses. The dollar is unchanged at +1 and the reasoning is unchanged with it. August payrolls printed +162,000 against a +53,000 consensus with the prior two months revised up by a combined 55,000, unemployment held 4.1%, average hourly earnings +0.3% monthly and 3.1% annually, participation rose to 61.6%. That removed the labour-market-collapse premise behind the dovish case and took the 2-year yield to its highest since January 2025 and the 10-year to about 4.78%. CME FedWatch now carries roughly 66% for a September 16 hike to 4.00% with fed funds futures nearer 60%, and TE's own forecast for the meeting is 4.00%. It stays at +1 rather than going to +2 because Waller's hold case was conditioned on inflation, citing three-month annualised core PCE at 3.05% against 4.76% in February, and Friday's CPI is what resolves it. DXY 99.147, essentially flat. Canada holds +1 with the split from Friday intact but the balance shifting back toward the commodity leg. The central-bank leg is still the broken one - August employment fell 41,700 against a +15,000 consensus after +75,100, full-time down 35,900, wage growth decelerating to 2.0% annual from 2.8% - while the policy rate stays 2.25% after a seventh consecutive hold on September 2 in which the BoC flagged stronger upside inflation risks from the war and from tariffs. The oil leg, though, keeps getting stronger: WTI is 92.826 this morning, up 1.47% on the session and 8.24% on the week, with Brent at 97.770 and up 1.55%. USD/CAD stays a RANGE at 1.38347 rather than reverting to a short, and the C$27.6 billion of Canadian counter-tariffs across roughly 700 US product lines take effect tomorrow. Australia is unchanged at +2 and is the least disturbed position on this board. The cash rate is 4.35%, the G10 high, re-verified on TE this morning and held at the August 11 meeting whose minutes described inflation as too high and excess demand as persistent while explicitly listing Middle East oil prices among the arguments for a 25bp hike. September 29 sits near 54%, trimmed mean is stuck at 3.6%, headline eased to 3.5%, and annual GDP growth at 2.1% remains above the RBA's estimated 2% speed limit. AUD/USD 0.72075. AUD/NZD is 1.22681 and remains the best-working idea here. New Zealand stays at 0 - OCR 2.75% after a second consecutive hike on September 2, the highest headline inflation on the board at 4.1%, unemployment at a decade high of 5.6% - and Switzerland stays at +1, with the policy rate at 0%, August CPI at 0.8% and Q2 annual growth revised to 2.3%, but capped by an SNB that named Middle East tensions as a franc-strengthening risk and signalled greater readiness to intervene. Finally the war, which did what this file said it would do at the open. Oil gapped higher on the weekend escalation: the US struck three Iranian tankers in retaliation for ballistic missiles fired at US Navy warships on September 5, Iran claimed a strike on an unmanned US vessel entering Hormuz on September 6 which US Central Command dismissed as a total lie, and Tehran has said it will declare a RESTRICTED maritime zone beyond the Strait within days while warning of a more painful response. Hormuz traffic has fallen to its lowest since May. What capped the rally rather than extending it is that the restricted-zone announcement is being read as a substitute for physical closure, and the US has cleared the strait of mines and degraded Iran's ability to re-lay them, with workarounds expanding. USOIL stays LONG at MEDIUM rather than being upgraded.

USD.note: TE re-verified this morning: policy rate 3.75% upper bound, CPI 3.4% with MoM 0.1%, unemployment 4.1% in August, non-farm payrolls +162,000 with the prior month revised to +21,000 from -23,000, Q2 GDP 1.5% annualised and 2.1% annual, average hourly earnings +0.3% m/m and 3.1% y/y, participation 61.6%, private payrolls +127,000, government +35,000, job vacancies 7,738k from 6,948k, initial claims 206k, business confidence 54.6, manufacturing PMI 53.9, non-manufacturing 55.4, services 56.5, consumer confidence 51.7, retail sales -0.6% m/m. USD HOLDS at +1, unchanged from yesterday, and nothing this morning tests it. The August jobs report removed the premise of the dovish case rather than merely offsetting it - the argument for a soft dollar had rested on a labour market that printed MINUS 23,000 in July, and the report tripled a +53,000 consensus while revising the prior two months up by a combined 55,000 and turning July positive, with participation rising while unemployment held, which is absorption rather than deterioration. The 2-year yield reached its highest since January 2025 and the 10-year is around 4.78%, the highest since November 2023. The July FOMC minutes carried on TE add to this: policymakers generally viewed inflation risks as tilted to the upside, several judged financial conditions may not be restrictive enough, and a small group supported raising rates in July outright - though TE also notes the meeting predated the cooler employment and inflation data, so the minutes may overstate current expectations. The upgrade still stops at +1 for one specific reason: Governor Waller conditioned his public case for a HOLD on inflation continuing to improve, citing three-month annualised core PCE at 3.05% against 4.76% in February, and explicitly not on the monthly payroll number. Chair Warsh has warned separately that better summer inflation readings do not yet show meaningful improvement in the underlying trend. The meeting is two-sided and the resolving input is US CPI on Friday September 11 at 12:30Z, consensus 3.4%, preceded by PPI on the 10th.

catalysts.note: UK 10-year gilts at a post-2008 5.25% and 30-year at 5.89%, the highest since May 1998; German 10-year at its highest since 2011; Japan 10-year at 3% for the first time since 1996; US 10-year near 4.78%. The FX read depends entirely on the driver - Japan's move is normalisation and yen-positive, the UK's is fiscal and sterling-negative. This distinction is the basis of today's GBP downgrade.

The SNB signalled in June a greater readiness to intervene in FX markets, naming Middle East tensions as something that could strengthen the franc. That is the stated ceiling keeping CHF at +1 despite two upside data surprises, and the pending Hormuz restricted zone is exactly the scenario the Bank described.

geopolitics: Oil opened bid on Monday exactly as flagged, but the rally was capped rather than extended, and the reason why is the most important nuance in the war right now. WTI is 92.826, up 1.47% on the session and 8.24% on the week; Brent is 97.770, up 1.55%. The escalation that produced it: on September 5 the IRGC fired ballistic missiles toward a US aircraft carrier and a destroyer - neither hit - and US forces struck three Iranian oil tankers in response under the tanker-for-tanker policy. On September 6 Iran claimed it had struck an unmanned US vessel attempting to enter the Strait of Hormuz, a claim the US military dismissed as a total lie. Tehran has now said it will declare a RESTRICTED maritime zone beyond the Strait within days, warning of a more painful response to the naval blockade. Hormuz traffic has fallen to its lowest level since May despite US Navy escort operations. What capped the price move is that the market is reading the restricted-zone announcement as a SUBSTITUTE for physical closure rather than a step toward it: shipping through the Strait has been largely blocked since the air war began on February 28, the US has since cleared the strait of mines and materially degraded Iran's ability to re-lay them, and workarounds are expanding, which steadily reduces both the strategic importance of the Strait and the leverage Tehran holds over it. The Institute for the Study of War assesses that the IRGC faction controlling decision-making is dissatisfied with the trajectory of the war and intent on changing it by force, with US intelligence assessing Iran may be considering a significant escalation - so the tail risk is fatter even as the base case premium stops widening. Five FX consequences follow. First, the Canadian dollar is now a single-legged trade: with employment down 41,700 and wage growth decelerating to 2.0% y/y, the BoC leg is broken and crude is doing all the work, which keeps CAD at +1, keeps USD/CAD a range rather than a short, and makes GBP/CAD the better way to trade Canada because the sterling side supplies the second leg. Second, the tightening board rests on this shock and the central banks say so explicitly - the RBA's August minutes list Middle East conflict driving oil prices FIRST among the arguments for a hike, the BoC's September statement flags the continuation of the war as an upside inflation risk, the RBNZ attributes 4.1% inflation largely to Middle East fuel prices, and the ECB accounts cite Middle East upside risk. That is four reaction functions running off one input, which is why the whole board is hawkish and also why it would all reprice together on a de-escalation. Third, the franc ceiling becomes more relevant, not less: a haven bid into a restricted-zone declaration is precisely the scenario the SNB described in June when it signalled greater readiness to intervene, which is why CHF stays capped at +1 and every CHF cross stays at MEDIUM or below. Fourth, the yen's terms-of-trade problem keeps deteriorating - Japan imports essentially all its oil, the trade balance is MINUS 634 billion yen, the current account swung to MINUS 92.3 billion, and July household spending fell 3.6% year-on-year with energy and food named as the cause - so the BoJ is hiking into a shock that strengthens its inflation argument while eroding its demand base, which is exactly why tonight's cash earnings print matters more than anything else this week. Fifth, and this is the connection to today's sterling downgrade: the oil shock is what is feeding the global bond rout, and the rout is hitting currencies differently depending on whether their yields are rising for policy reasons or fiscal ones. Japan's 10-year at 3% for the first time since 1996 is normalisation and is yen-positive; the UK's 10-year at a post-2008 5.25% and 30-year at 5.89% is fiscal and is sterling-negative. Same shock, opposite FX signs.
